content: Immediate initiation of treatment can save lives and should not be delayed while awaiting confirmatory test results. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-certainty evidence. To enhance the accuracy of nucleic acid-based diagnostic tests for infants, an indeterminate range of viral copy equivalents should be utilized. This recommendation is strong and based on moderate-certainty evidence. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. For children aged 18 months or older who are suspected of having HIV or have been exposed to HIV, serological testing should follow the standard diagnostic algorithm used for adults. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence. However, caregiver-assisted testing using HIV self-testing kits for children aged 18 months and older is not currently recommended. In high HIV-burden settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics should be routinely tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. Similarly, in such settings, HIV testing should be offered to infants and children with unknown HIV status in outpatient or immunization clinics. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. Network-based testing, including testing the biological children of people with HIV and within social networks, is recommended. This includes family and household testing services and partner services. These approaches are strongly recommended with moderate-certainty evidence. National regulatory agencies are encouraged to adopt point-of-care early infant diagnosis (EID) without delays for further evaluations, streamlining registration and approval processes for immediate implementation. For couples and partners, network-based testing is recommended, including social network testing, family and household testing services, and partner services. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. Partner services for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) should be offered as part of a comprehensive package of voluntary STI testing, care, and prevention. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. Coercive or forced testing is never justified. STI partner services should offer a range of options based on patient preferences, feasibility, and available resources. These options include patient referral, enhanced patient referral, delayed provider referral, provider-patient referral, provider-assisted referral, and social network approaches. Provider-supported approaches are particularly effective and should be prioritized where feasible. Expedited partner therapy (EPT) may also be considered for some curable STIs, such as chlamydia or gonorrhea. Linkage to STI management services for sexual partners is an essential component of STI services, and these services should be integrated into broader health programs. Women who disclose intimate partner violence or sexual assault should be offered immediate support. At a minimum, healthcare providers should offer first-line support when violence is disclosed. Knowledge of one’s own and one’s partner’s HIV status is critical for an effective HIV response. The primary goals of HIV testing services (HTS) are to deliver accurate diagnoses promptly and facilitate access to prevention, treatment, and care services. Globally, access to HTS has significantly increased. In 2005, only 12% of people who wanted to test for HIV could do so. By the end of 2022, an estimated 86% of people with HIV knew their status. Several countries, including Botswana, Eswatini, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe, have achieved the “95-95-95” targets: 95% of people living with HIV know their status, 95% of those who know their status are on ART, and 95% of those on treatment are virally suppressed. However, gaps remain, particularly among key populations, adult men, partners of people living with HIV, adolescents, and children. HTS programs must focus on populations most affected by HIV and at high ongoing risk, as well as those critical to achieving and sustaining low HIV incidence. Countries should use data to refine their responses, focusing prevention strategies on groups and locations that would yield the highest impact. Integration of HTS into other health services is increasingly important, as it is cost-effective and provides client-centered care. Tools such as dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests and self-tests offer unique opportunities for service integration. Despite progress, significant gaps remain in linkage to and retention in care, particularly for key populations, men, young people, children, and those previously diagnosed with HIV but not on ART. Misdiagnosis of HIV status can occur due to suboptimal testing algorithms, outdated strategies, and poor-quality testing. Quality management systems (QMS) are essential and should be expanded alongside HTS scale-up. Key populations, including men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, and people in prisons, are disproportionately affected by HIV. Barriers to HTS uptake include stigma, discrimination, criminalization, and punitive laws. Men, in particular, are less likely than women to know their HIV status, be on treatment, or achieve viral suppression. This disparity is most pronounced in sub-Saharan Africa, where HIV-related morbidity and mortality rates are higher among men. Adolescents and young people are also underserved. In high HIV-burden settings, nearly 90% of HIV-positive adolescents live in eastern and southern Africa. Testing coverage among adolescents remains low, with only 25% of girls and 17% of boys aged 15–19 tested for HIV in the past year. Efforts must focus on improving access for adolescents, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where HIV incidence remains high among young women and girls. HIV testing coverage among children is often low, despite high positivity rates in clinical settings. Early infant diagnosis (EID) rates remain suboptimal, with only 60% of infants receiving an HIV nucleic acid test within the first two months of life in 2019. Delays in obtaining results and further losses in the treatment cascade result in less than one-third of perinatally infected infants being linked to services and initiating ART in a timely manner. These guidelines aim to address gaps in HTS and provide evidence-based recommendations to support countries in achieving low HIV incidence by 2030. They emphasize the importance of integrating HTS into broader health services, ensuring quality testing, and linking individuals to prevention, treatment, and care. The guidelines are intended for national HIV program managers, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders involved in HTS implementation. They advocate for a public health and human rights-based approach to HTS, ensuring services are accessible, acceptable, and of high quality.
